name: Islamic Republic of Pakistan
info: The Islamic Republic of Pakistan, proclaimed in 1956, is a nuclear-armed South Asian state of 241 million people, shaped by wars with India over Kashmir, the secession of Bangladesh and alternating military and civilian rule.

facts.founder: Muhammad Ali Jinnah, founder of Pakistan and its first governor-general; the republic of 1956 succeeded the dominion he had led
facts.predecessor: Dominion of Pakistan (1947–1956), a monarchy within the Commonwealth created by the partition of British India

t: Pakistan was created on 14 August 1947 by the partition of British India, in riots that killed between 200,000 and 2,000,000 people and the largest migration in history; it adopted a republican constitution in 1956 and became an Islamic republic of two provinces, East and West Pakistan.

East Pakistan seceded as Bangladesh in 1971 after a nine-month war in which independent researchers estimate 300,000 to 500,000 civilians died; the loss drove Pakistan to build the nuclear weapons it tested in 1998, the seventh state to do so.
Military coups in 1958, 1977 and 1999 put generals in power for three long stretches, and the first transfer from one elected government to another came only in May 2013.
dyk: The name Pakistan was coined in January 1933 by the activist Choudhry Rahmat Ali in a pamphlet, Now or Never, as an acronym of Panjab, Afghania, Kashmir, Sindh and Baluchistan; in Persian and Urdu it also means 'the land of the pure'.
ev: Pakistan adopts a republican constitution and becomes an Islamic republic with two geographically separate provinces, East Pakistan and West Pakistan.
President Iskander Mirza imposes martial law and is succeeded by General Ayub Khan, who suspends the constitution; a presidential constitution follows in 1962.
After the military refuses to transfer power to the Awami League and launches Operation Searchlight, war with India ends in defeat and East Pakistan becomes Bangladesh.
A military coup against Zulfikar Ali Bhutto's Pakistan Peoples Party ends democracy; General Zia-ul-Haq becomes president in 1978 and Islamises law and the economy.
Nawaz Sharif authorises nuclear tests in answer to India's, making Pakistan the seventh nuclear-armed state.
The Kargil War brings Pakistan and India to the brink, and General Pervez Musharraf takes power in a bloodless coup.
After Benazir Bhutto's assassination in 2007 the Pakistan Peoples Party wins the election; Musharraf resigns on 18 August and Asif Ali Zardari succeeds him.
The Pakistan Muslim League (N) wins the general election and Nawaz Sharif becomes prime minister for the third time, in the first successful democratic transition.

sections.foundation:
The Indus plain held Mehrgarh, the cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation and Gandhara, and official chronology dates the foundation of Pakistan to Muhammad ibn Qasim's conquest of Sindh in 711. Britain took Karachi in 1839 and Sindh in 1843 and by 1893 ruled the whole region. Sir Syed Ahmed Khan's two-nation theory led to the All-India Muslim League in 1906, and under Muhammad Ali Jinnah the Lahore Resolution of 1940 demanded a separate state. The League won 90 percent of the Muslim seats in 1946, and on 3 June 1947 Lord Mountbatten announced partition. Pakistan was established on 14 August 1947 from the Muslim-majority provinces of the north-west and East Bengal. In the Punjab riots between 200,000 and 2,000,000 people were killed; some 6.5 million Muslims moved to West Pakistan and 4.7 million Hindus and Sikhs to India, the largest migration in human history, and a dispute over Jammu and Kashmir brought war with India in 1947–1948.

Jinnah became the first governor-general and died of tuberculosis on 11 September 1948; Liaquat Ali Khan was the first prime minister. From 1947 to 1956 Pakistan was a monarchy within the Commonwealth under two monarchs. The Objectives Resolution of March 1949 affirmed that sovereignty over the universe belongs to God alone, and it became the preamble of the constitutions of 1956, 1962 and 1973. The constitution of 1956 made Pakistan an Islamic republic of two provinces, East and West Pakistan, separated by the breadth of India.
sections.socioeconomy:
Pakistan is the fifth most populous country, with more than 241.5 million people in 2023 and the second-largest Muslim population in the world; 96.35 percent are Muslim, 2.17 percent Hindu and 1.37 percent Christian. By the 2023 census Punjabis are 36.98 percent, Pashtuns 18.15 and Sindhis 14.31 of a people speaking 75 to 85 languages, with Urdu and English official. A diaspora of seven to ten million sent home $38.3 billion in 2024–25. Literacy was 62.3 percent in 2018, with wide regional and gender gaps, and the state spends 2.3 percent of GDP on education, among the lowest in the region; about one in six girls is married in childhood.

The economy ranks 26th in the world by purchasing power and 42nd by nominal GDP, $450 billion in 2026, or $1,840 a head. Agriculture employs 43.5 percent of the labour force: Pakistan is the seventh wheat producer, fourth in cotton and milk and fifth in sugar. Textiles contribute 9.5 percent of GDP and employ some 15 million; services make 58.42 percent of GDP, and ICT exports reached a record $2.6 billion in 2023–24 with three million freelancers. Beneath lie the fifth-largest coal reserves in the world and the Reko Diq copper and gold deposit. Yet 44.7 percent of the population live below $4.20 a day, growth of 2.5 percent in 2024 was the second lowest in South Asia, women's economic participation ranks near the bottom of the world and the trade deficit was $21.3 billion in 2023.
sections.military:
Pakistan has the world's seventh-largest standing armed forces, about 660,000 active troops and 291,000 paramilitary personnel in 2024, in an Army, Navy and Air Force that have wielded significant influence over politics since 1947. The National Command Authority controls the nuclear arsenal under a doctrine of full-spectrum deterrence. The nuclear programme began in 1972 after the loss of East Pakistan, Abdul Qadeer Khan founded the Kahuta Research Laboratories in 1976 to enrich uranium, and India's tests in May 1998 were answered with Pakistan's own, making it the seventh nuclear-armed state. The United States, Turkey and China supply its equipment.

Four conventional wars have been fought with India: the Kashmir war of 1947–1948, which left Pakistan a third of the region; 1965; 1971, when India's support for the Bengali Mukti Bahini ended in Indian victory and the independence of Bangladesh; and the Kargil War of 1999. The Inter-Services Intelligence, founded within a year of independence, channelled American resources to the Afghan mujahideen against the Soviet Union and later helped establish the Taliban. Since 2001 the army has fought the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa; by its own reckoning the war on terrorism has cost up to $118 billion, over 81,000 casualties and 1.8 million displaced civilians. In September 2025 a Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement extended Pakistan's nuclear umbrella to Saudi Arabia.
sections.governance:
Pakistan is a federal parliamentary republic with Islam as the state religion. Its constitutions of 1956 and 1962 were each swept away by generals, and the 1973 constitution written under Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, which declared an Islamic Republic whose laws must conform to the Quran and Sunnah, was suspended by Zia-ul-Haq's martial law in 1977 and restored with amendments in 1985. Military rulers governed de facto as presidents in 1958–1971, 1977–1988 and 1999–2008; Zia instituted Shariat courts, and the Ahmadis have been barred from calling themselves Muslims since 1974.

Today the president is a ceremonial head of state chosen by an electoral college. The National Assembly has 336 members, 70 seats reserved for women and religious minorities, and the 96-member Senate gives the four provinces, Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Sindh and Balochistan, equal weight. Benazir Bhutto became the first woman prime minister in 1988, and power alternated between her Pakistan Peoples Party and Nawaz Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League (N) until Musharraf's coup; the first democratic transition came in May 2013, Imran Khan's PTI won in 2018, and Shehbaz Sharif took office after a no-confidence vote in 2022 and again in 2024. All sex outside marriage is a crime, male homosexuality carries up to ten years, hundreds of women die each year in honour killings, and Reporters Without Borders ranked the press 158th of 180 in 2025.
sections.impact:
Pakistan is a middle power and a declared nuclear-weapon state, a member of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and a major non-NATO ally of the United States since 2004. Its founders sought to lead the Muslim world, and though their 'Islamistan' found no takers, the OIC they wanted was formed in the 1970s; Pakistan backed independence movements from Indonesia to Algeria and championed the Palestinian cause. China calls it an 'Iron Brother': China is its largest trading partner and the builder of Gwadar port and the China–Pakistan Economic Corridor. Relations with Washington have been 'on-and-off', from Cold War alliance to sanctions over the nuclear programme and mistrust during the twenty-year war in Afghanistan.

Kashmir divides the subcontinent: India holds about 45.1 percent, Pakistan 38.2 and China 20, along a Line of Control drawn in 1949, and three of the four Indo-Pakistani wars were fought over it. Pakistan sheltered millions of Afghans after the Soviet invasion, sustained the mujahideen and the Taliban, and ordered undocumented Afghans expelled in October 2023. In culture the national poet Muhammad Iqbal shaped Urdu letters, Abdus Salam won the Nobel Prize in Physics and Malala Yousafzai became the youngest Nobel laureate; Pakistan launched the first satellite of any Muslim nation in 1990 and has won every major ICC cricket tournament.
sections.decline:
Pakistan's politics since 2008 have been civilian but unsteady. Musharraf resigned under threat of impeachment on 18 August 2008; the Pakistan Peoples Party governed until the Pakistan Muslim League (N) won in 2013 and Nawaz Sharif returned. Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf won in 2018 and lost a no-confidence vote in April 2022; in the election of 2024 PTI-backed independents formed the largest bloc, yet Shehbaz Sharif was elected prime minister by a coalition of the PML (N) and PPP. The military's influence persists, and Freedom House rated internet freedom 'Not Free' in 2024.

The economy is the pressing weakness. Growth of 2.5 percent in 2024 was the second lowest in South Asia, 44.7 percent of Pakistanis live below the international poverty line, 16.5 percent in extreme poverty, and the trade deficit stood at $21.3 billion in 2023; the country scored 27 of 100 on the Corruption Perceptions Index in 2024 and ranks near the bottom for women's economic participation. Terrorism continues in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where the army has fought the Tehrik-e-Taliban since 2001. Against this stand remittances of $38.3 billion, ICT exports and freelancers earning nearly $1 billion in foreign exchange, nuclear and hydroelectric power, the untapped coal and the Reko Diq mine, and new weight abroad: the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia of September 2025 makes an attack on either an attack on both.

summary: The Islamic Republic of Pakistan, proclaimed in 1956 in the state carved from British India in 1947, lost East Pakistan as Bangladesh in 1971, answered India with nuclear weapons in 1998 and has swung between generals and elected governments, a middle power of 241 million people tied to China and Saudi Arabia and still facing poverty, terrorism and the dispute over Kashmir.
references: Ian Talbot, Pakistan: A New History (Hurst, 2012)
Ayesha Jalal, The Struggle for Pakistan: A Muslim Homeland and Global Politics (Harvard University Press, 2014)

pointDescs.1956: The republican constitution makes Pakistan an Islamic republic of East and West Pakistan, nine years after independence.
pointDescs.1958: Martial law under Iskander Mirza gives way to General Ayub Khan, who suspends the constitution and in 1962 adopts a presidential system.
pointDescs.1965: Years of significant growth end with the second war with India, which brings an economic downturn and public discontent by 1967.
pointDescs.1969: Yahya Khan consolidates control as a cyclone kills 500,000 in East Pakistan; the Awami League wins the first democratic elections of 1970.
pointDescs.1971: Operation Searchlight and the war with India end in defeat; East Pakistan becomes Bangladesh and the nuclear programme is launched in 1972.
pointDescs.1977: A coup ends democracy; Zia-ul-Haq becomes president in 1978, Islamises the state and makes Pakistan the conduit for American aid to the Afghan mujahideen.
pointDescs.1988: Zia dies in a plane crash and Benazir Bhutto becomes the first woman prime minister, after a decade in which Pakistan was among South Asia's fastest-growing economies.
pointDescs.1998: Nawaz Sharif's government tests nuclear weapons in reply to India, making Pakistan the seventh nuclear-armed state.
pointDescs.1999: The Kargil War and civil-military turmoil bring Pervez Musharraf to power in a bloodless coup.
pointDescs.2008: Musharraf resigns on 18 August after the Pakistan Peoples Party's victory; the war on terrorism is costing the country tens of billions and tens of thousands of casualties.
pointDescs.2013: The Pakistan Muslim League (N) wins and Nawaz Sharif returns as prime minister in the first successful democratic transition.
pointDescs.2018: Imran Khan's PTI wins the general election; he is ousted by a no-confidence vote in April 2022.
pointDescs.2025: Shehbaz Sharif's coalition governs after the disputed 2024 election; the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement extends Pakistan's nuclear umbrella to Saudi Arabia.

notes: The saved article's Bibliography and Further reading sections contain only empty headings, so references is [].
The register's start year 1956 is the republican constitution; the state itself dates from 14 August 1947 (the dominion), treated in 'foundation' and 'predecessor'.

The 1971 death toll is given as the article gives it: 300,000–500,000 by independent researchers, 3 million by the Bangladesh government, 'now nearly universally regarded as excessively inflated'; the profile uses the researchers' range.

The curve's peak is placed at 1965, before the second war with India, when the state still held East Pakistan and the article records 'significant growth' under the 1962 presidential system; the nuclear tests of 1998 are set at 8 on a smaller territory.
The article gives the diaspora as 'around 10 million' (Economy) and 'approximately 7 million' (Diaspora); both figures appear as a range.
Population figures: 'over 241.5 million' (lead, 2023) is used; the article's GDP figures are 'as of 2026'.
